summary: Verified against the code. OpenShorts is a long-video to 9:16 clip farm (Opus Clip-style), not a polishing editor for talking-head reels. What exists and works: word-timestamp ASR; Gemini (or a local OpenAI-compatible LLM for the text passes) picks 15-60 s moments; clip boundaries snap to words and silence; MediaPipe/YOLO face-tracking reframe; captions auto-burned by libass in one default karaoke style; a hook text card; a Gemini edit decision list compiled to a clamped FFmpeg chain; a manual word-snapped EDL recut editor; an MCP server over HTTP and stdio plus a Claude skill; social publishing. "HyperFrames graphics" is false: zero matches in the tree or in any file read. Against the user's four problems: no automatic silence, filler or retake removal; no color grading; captions at exactly the "active word turns yellow + pop" tier the user rejects; no stock B-roll; no motion-graphics system. On the user's question: taking OpenShorts would not make autobroll's captions premium like Captions.ai. Its captions are the same class or simpler, one default style with at most four active-word effects, no emoji and no LLM emphasis. Its donor value is plumbing: the ASR contract, a clean libass karaoke writer, word-snapping, and the "LLM emits an edit decision list, deterministic code compiles FFmpeg" pattern. The premium caption engine still has to be built.
captions_detail: Verified in subtitles.py. generate_ass() builds blocks with _collect_word_blocks (max_chars, max_duration). Each word gets its own Dialogue event, the whole block stays visible, and the active word gets an inline override prefix followed by {\r}. The effect options are exactly: none (colour only); glow (\3c plus \bord at least 3 plus \blur4); box (thick coloured \bord, \blur0); and pop (\fscx90 to 108 over 110 ms via \t). base_opacity dims inactive words by scaling RGB (factor 0.5+0.5*opacity) rather than using alpha. There is an optional BorderStyle 3 background box, alignment top/middle/bottom, SAFE_MARGIN_V=43 at PlayResY 288, and a per-event {\an5} prefix inside SPLIT-layout ranges. main.py auto_caption_clip (line 1068) burns AUTO_CAPTION_STYLE on every clip by default (Anton, uppercase, white text, active word #FFE500, 4 px black border, pop, 16 chars / 1.4 s, base_opacity 1.0); AUTO_CAPTIONS=0 turns it off. There are THREE caption renderers, not two: libass subtitles.py; remotion/src/compositions/Subtitles.tsx for the server render-service; and dashboard/src/remotion/compositions/Subtitles.tsx for the Player preview and renderInBrowser. The two Remotion copies have diverged: only the dashboard copy implements baseOpacity dimming (factor 0.35+0.65, which differs from libass) and uppercase. Remotion animations are none, word-highlight (glow), pop (spring) and karaoke (pill), with positions top 12%, middle 45% and bottom 10%. The MCP add_subtitles tool exposes only classic|karaoke, position, font, colours and uppercase, with no effect parameter. Absent everywhere: emoji in captions (emoji rendering exists only in hooks.py's static PIL hook card), LLM-chosen emphasis or keyword colouring, per-word entrance variety, multi-colour styles, a named preset library, line balancing, and word-synced SFX. Verdict: basic karaoke tier, not Captions.ai/Submagic level.
motion_graphics_detail: There is no motion-graphics engine or template library, and HyperFrames is absent. What exists: (1) One graphic template, the hook card. hooks.py create_hook_image renders it as a static PIL PNG in six HOOK_STYLES (classic, dark, yellow, red, outline, outline_yellow) with emoji runs, burned with an FFmpeg overlay and no animation. The Remotion HookOverlay.tsx adds spring, fade and slide-up entrances. (2) Gemini edit-decision-list effects compiled by edit_builder.py: zoom_in, punch_in and zoom_pulse become zoompan terms; color_pop, bw_moment, flash and vignette become time-gated eq, hue and vignette filters. Hard caps: 12 edits, max zoom 0.15, no overlapping zooms, at most 2 flashes, and zooms dropped when captions are already burned in. A second Gemini prompt (get_effects_config) drives the Remotion VideoEffects.tsx CSS zoom and filter segments. (3) punch_in.py audio-beat crop pushes (max 1.12x, 18 s minimum gap), which are OFF by default (PUNCH_IN=0). There is no kinetic typography, animated stats, icons, lower thirds, UI mockups, SFX or music logic, and no LLM-authored graphics code.
llm_integration_detail: Every creative decision inside the pipeline is a Gemini call (google-genai): moment picking in main.get_viral_clips and clip_selection, layout_picker.py (frames), screencast detection, the silent-video vision path, editor.py (effects decision list and Remotion EffectsConfig, plus a legacy _repair_filter), hook_grounding.py, thumbnails and SaaSShorts. llm_backend.py sends only the transcript scoring and detail passes to an OpenAI-compatible /chat/completions endpoint (json_schema, then json_object, then none, with pydantic validation); its docstring says the vision paths stay on Gemini. Without a Gemini key and without LLM_BASE_URL, process_video is rejected (app.py:2744). There is no Claude API, Claude Agent SDK, Claude Code CLI or Codex CLI integration. Outward agent surface: mcp_server.py is a hand-rolled JSON-RPC MCP server with no MCP SDK. It is not dependency-free: it is a FastAPI APIRouter that uses httpx.ASGITransport to call back into the app in-process. It exposes eight tools: process_video, create_upload, get_job_status, list_clips, get_quota, add_subtitles, recut_clip, publish_clip. SKILL.md still says seven. mcp_stdio.py redirects stdout to stderr before importing app and runs the app's lifespan; its docstring documents `claude mcp add openshorts -- python mcp_stdio.py`. Cloud OAuth goes through cloud/mcp_oauth.py and falls under the commercial license. Limits for an external brain: the MCP layer does not expose word-level transcripts (the REST route at app.py:3721 does), and recut_clip is capped at 12 segments of at least 0.5 s each. So Claude Code or Codex can orchestrate coarse actions (clip a URL, restyle, recut, publish) but cannot make fine-grained cut or caption decisions through it. The pattern worth copying is edit_builder.py: the LLM emits a validated edit decision list and stdlib-only code compiles it with hard caps.

license_risks:
The repo code is MIT. The risks come from what it pulls in.
(1) MatAnyone2Kit (GPL-3.0) with MatAnyone2 and EdgeSAM weights under the S-Lab non-commercial license (native/README.md lines 43-45 and 114-117). Correction: it is NOT built at install time. postinstall only rebuilds node-pty and runs _scripts/build-camera.cjs, which bundles LiveKit and MediaPipe under Apache-2.0. MatAnyone is an opt-in `npm run build:matting` (_scripts/build-matanyone.cjs git-clones flowtyone/MatAnyone2Kit). The exposure applies only if you build or ship the matting feature. Drop it for a commercial product.
(2) The hyperframes npm dependency (^0.6.121, heygen-com/hyperframes) is Apache-2.0, but its registry components load GSAP 3.14.2 from the jsDelivr CDN (verified in caption-pill-karaoke.html). GSAP uses Webflow's standard no-charge license, which is not OSI-approved and excludes tools that compete with Webflow's visual or no-code animation products. An AI tool that generates motion graphics is a gray area worth legal review.
(3) Remotion is not a dependency. SKILL.md only lists it as an engine the agent may choose per animation slot. If the LLM chooses it, Remotion's license applies: free for individuals and companies of up to 3 employees, paid company license above that. This exposure is indirect but real, because the choice is left to the LLM.
(4) Proprietary paid services called at runtime: the HeyGen audio library API (SFX and music), NVIDIA Studio Voice NIM (gRPC), Upload-Post, and ElevenLabs as an optional fallback.
(5) Vendored LiveKit track-processors and MediaPipe wasm/tflite (Apache-2.0, THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES present) and xterm and node-pty (MIT) are fine.
stack: Electron 33 desktop app with a CommonJS Node main process and a vanilla JS/HTML renderer. Capture is macOS-only. node-pty and xterm provide an embedded agent terminal. Background matting uses optional Swift/Core ML (MatAnyone2Kit), with a LiveKit/MediaPipe fallback. The editing engine is a modified fork of browser-use/video-use kept in video-use/: Python helpers that call ffmpeg/ffprobe, faster-whisper and PIL. Graphics come from HyperFrames (npm; HTML plus GSAP rendered by headless Chrome), with Manim, Remotion and PIL listed as options in SKILL.md. SFX and music come from the HeyGen API, voice cleanup from NVIDIA NIM, and publishing from Upload-Post.

summary:
VibeTube is a macOS screen-plus-webcam recorder for YouTube tutorials. It hands each recorded project folder to Claude Code or Codex CLI, and the agent edits by following a bundled, heavily modified copy of browser-use's video-use skill.

What checks out:
- The provider and agent harness is real and well built (providers.js, agent.js).
- render.py adds real ffmpeg work on top of upstream: multicam layouts, crossfades with timeline remapping, a slow continuous zoom, 9:16 reframing, SFX on word timestamps, sidechain music ducking and VP9 alpha overlays.

What is weaker than the first evaluation said:
1. Those render features run only in multicam mode, which needs both a `screen` and a `cam` source. The app has no way to import existing footage; clips come only from its own recorder. A single-file talking-head reel goes through the plain upstream single-source path: no zoom, no crossfade, no reframing.
2. The compose and iterate prompts never ask for silence or filler removal. Retake removal is prompted only when a script.md exists, and every boundary defaults to a 0.4 s crossfade, which works against tight reel cuts.
3. Built-in captions are upstream video-use's static two-word UPPERCASE Helvetica SRT, with no active-word highlight. The 9:16 "Hormozi" captions are only a prompt telling the LLM to adapt a HyperFrames caption-* example on every run.
4. Motion graphics: zero templates ship in the repo. Every graphic is LLM-authored HyperFrames HTML/GSAP, used mostly as full-frame cutaways.
5. There is no stock B-roll and no timeline editor.
6. The color grade, packed transcript and timeline view are unmodified upstream files.

Best value: the CLI provider layer and the VibeTube-original render.py compositing code.

fit_rationale:
A poor base, a selective donor.
- Wrong product: VibeTube is a macOS screen-plus-webcam recorder for 16:9 tutorials. It cannot import existing footage; append-clip only accepts buffers the app recorded itself.
- Its best render features need a screen source: multicam layouts, zoom, crossfades and 9:16 reframing all run only in multicam mode. A single talking-head file goes through the plain upstream single-source path.
- Opposite philosophy: its editing inverts the user's principle that deterministic tools do the heavy lifting. Cuts, captions and graphics are all decided and authored by the LLM from prompt text on every run.
- Missing pieces: no silence, filler or retake detector, no premium caption engine, no stock B-roll, no timeline.
- Worth taking: electron/providers.js and agent.js, the Claude Code/Codex layer (small Electron port needed). From render.py: the crossfade timeline remap, alpha overlay compositing and SFX/music mixing. grade.py, the packed transcript and the timeline view are better taken from upstream browser-use/video-use, which is maintained and has the fps fix and tests.
captions_detail:
To the user's question (what if AutoBroll has captions, but not premium ones like Captions.ai): VibeTube does not fill that gap either.

Its own caption code is render.py build_master_srt plus sub_force_style, the same style upstream video-use ships:
- two-word UPPERCASE chunks in Helvetica 18 Bold, white with a black outline
- burned with libass, placed higher on vertical video, or written as a sidecar .srt
- no active-word highlight, no per-word animation, no emphasis, no emoji, no presets

The "9:16 Hormozi captions" exist only as prompt text: electron/prompts.js lines 53-63 and the SKILL.md 'Subtitles' section. They tell the LLM to adapt a HyperFrames `caption-*` example to Whisper word times, render a transparent WebM and add it to the EDL overlays. The only real code on that path is the compositing: libvpx-vp9 decode so alpha survives, a PTS shift, and timing remapped across crossfades.

The real donor is upstream HyperFrames (heygen-com/hyperframes, Apache-2.0, about 52.7k stars, active; GSAP license caveat). It has 17 verified `caption-*` components: blend-difference, camera-follow, clip-wipe, editorial-emphasis, emoji-pop, glitch-rgb, gradient-fill, highlight, kinetic-slam, matrix-decode, neon-accent, neon-glow, parallax-layers, particle-burst, pill-karaoke, texture and weight-shift. Each embeds a words array of `{text, start, end}`, confirmed in caption-pill-karaoke.html and caption-emoji-pop.html, and animates each word with GSAP. That makes a deterministic premium path possible: inject the Whisper word JSON as data and render a transparent WebM once per style, instead of having the LLM rewrite the HTML on every run.

Caveats:
- The components are hard-coded to 1920x1080 and need 9:16 variants.
- They load Google Fonts and GSAP from CDNs.
- caption-emoji-pop's emoji logic is a 7-word demo dictionary (WORD_EMOJI), so emphasis and emoji picks must come from your own LLM step or a classifier and be passed in as data.
motion_graphics_detail:
The engine is HyperFrames (HTML/CSS/GSAP rendered in headless Chrome); SKILL.md also lists Manim, Remotion and PIL. VibeTube ships no templates. On each run the agent picks HyperFrames registry examples (the prompt names warm-grain, swiss-grid, kinetic-type, product-promo, logo-outro, lt-*, transitions-*, vfx-*, code-snippet-* and app-showcase) and fills them from the transcript. It times elements to Whisper words and renders each slot through a parallel sub-agent.

render.py inserts each graphic as a `graphic` layout: a full-frame cutaway with the voice continuing underneath and crossfades on either side. The prompt forbids overlaying graphics on the demo, so only captions and lower thirds would sit over the speaker.

What is deterministic in code:
- A slow linear zoom ramp (1.0 to 1.04/1.05) per range, multicam only. It is not a word-triggered punch.
- Crossfade transitions (fade, dissolve, slideleft, wiperight).
- Timeline remapping so overlays and SFX stay in sync after crossfades.
- SFX placed at LLM-chosen word times from the HeyGen library.
- Music ducked under the voice with sidechaincompress.

For pro-style reel B-roll (animated stats, kinetic type, lower thirds, UI mockups), the value lies in HyperFrames' own catalog (165 blocks, 224 components; for example count-up, data-chart, bar-chart-race, x-post, macos-notification), not in VibeTube.
llm_integration_detail:
The integration spawns the CLI as a subprocess and is swappable. settings.agentProvider is 'claude' or 'codex' (normalizeProvider).

Headless calls (providers.headlessArgs):
- Claude: `claude -p … --add-dir <cwd> --permission-mode bypassPermissions --output-format stream-json --verbose --max-turns N [--resume id]`
- Codex: `codex exec --sandbox workspace-write -c approval_policy="never" -c sandbox_workspace_write.network_access=true -c web_search="live" --json --skip-git-repo-check [resume <thread>] -- <prompt>`

The job runner (agent.runAgentJob):
- spawns the CLI detached, with keys from ~/.config/record-studio/.env or ~/Documents/avatar-muton/.env injected as environment variables
- parses stream-json or JSONL into progress events and captures session_id or thread_id per provider into project.json
- retries once without resume when the session is gone
- enforces a 15-minute idle timeout and a 3-hour cap, kills the whole process group, and cleans up orphans at startup
- decides success only by whether the final mp4 exists, so a stale final.mp4 lets a failed iterate pass

Instructions and interactive use:
- The brain's manual is video-use/SKILL.md, referenced through providers.skillContext.
- The per-project brief (prompts.montageBrief) goes into a managed block of CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md.
- A node-pty terminal runs the same CLI interactively: plan mode for Claude, on-request approvals for Codex.
- The model is inherited from the CLI config.

There is no MCP server and no typed tools. The agent drives ffmpeg and the Python helpers through raw shell.

stack: Python 3.10-3.12 with a Typer CLI and a pydantic JSON config schema. Captions are rendered in Playwright/Chromium, one RGBA PNG screenshot per word per narration state. Compositing and encoding use movielite, the author's own MIT library built on Numba, OpenCV and pictex/skia-python; it pipes bgr24 raw frames to ffmpeg libx264 yuv420p. Transcription uses openai-whisper (default model 'base', word_timestamps=True), with Google STT as an option. Optional extras: PictexSubtitleRenderer (html2pic, no browser) and two pywebview windows, a transcript editor and a CSS style previewer. The OpenAI SDK is not declared in any extra; it is imported lazily from ai/gpt.py.
size_note: Repo size is 731 KB. It has 131 .py files, not 95, totalling 256,299 bytes (about 6-7k LOC). There are 12 preset dirs, but `model` is an empty stub (0-byte pycaps.template.json, styles.css and main.py), so 11 presets are usable. It bundles 17 SFX mp3s and fonts (black.ttf in 5 presets, komika.ttf, PressStart2P.ttf). At runtime it downloads a 30.6 MB animated-emoji zip from the `emoji-assets-v2` GitHub release. Heavy dependencies: Playwright Chromium (~150 MB), and openai-whisper plus torch (GBs) unless you pass an external transcript.
summary:
pycaps only does captions: no cutting, color grade, stock B-roll or motion-graphics B-roll anywhere in the tree. The caption engine is real and wired end to end.

Pipeline: transcript, then splitters, then per-letter width measurement in Chromium, then line splitting at max_width_ratio, then structure tags (first/last word, line, segment) and semantic tags (regex, wordlist or AI), then text effects, then an optional pywebview editor, then the subtitle JSON is saved. Render: each word is screenshotted as an RGBA PNG for 5 narration states, with every tag and state as a CSS class. Motion is added afterwards in Python as position, scale and opacity functions on movielite clips: fade, pop, slide and zoom primitives with easing and manual overshoot, plus presets. These are triggered on narration start or end of a word, line or segment and filtered by boolean tag conditions. CSS animations are frozen (animations="disabled"). Other extras: typewriter (one bitmap per letter), LLM-chosen emoji per segment shown as animated Noto GIFs, a fixed emoji list after tagged words, and 17 tag-triggered SFX.

To the user's question (AutoBroll has captions, but not Captions.ai-level ones): pycaps is a real step up from "highlight one word gold". You get arbitrary CSS per word state, tag-driven emphasis, pop/zoom/slide with overshoot, emoji and SFX. It is still below Captions.ai or Submagic. Motion is only transform and opacity on static bitmaps. State changes are hard bitmap swaps with no color tween. No highlight box glides between words. There is no rotate, shake or blur. Placement is centered horizontally with only a top/center/bottom offset, and nothing is face- or safe-zone-aware. The presets are modest. AI emphasis and emoji are hard-wired to OpenAI gpt-4.1-mini or the proprietary pycaps.com API.

Re-verification confirmed most of the prior evaluation. It also turned up new bugs:
- A custom LLM subclass written to the Llm abstract signature breaks when injected.
- Custom SFX configs always crash the render.
- The emoji_in_word no-repeat option never works.
- TypewritingEffect passes a word state as the line state.
- WhisperX words without timestamps are silently dropped.
- `pip install pycaps` installs an unrelated PyPI project.

Activity has stalled since Feb 2026; the author's focus is now tscaps.
captions_detail:
Verified in code:
- Pipeline order is in pipeline/caps_pipeline.py (process_document, then render).
- renderer/renderer_page.py puts `.word`, `.word-N-in-line`, tag names and state classes on spans and line divs, so any Chromium CSS works, including @font-face from the template's resources dir.
- css_subtitle_renderer.py renders each word inside its full line, screenshots the bounding box via playwright_screenshot_capturer.py (omit_background, animations="disabled", scale="device"), and scales device_scale_factor with video height (reference 1280).
- rendered_image_cache.py keys the cache on word text plus only the CSS classes that appear in the template CSS, and ignores position by default. Unstyled states therefore share bitmaps, so it is usually 2-3 unique screenshots per word, not 5.
- Word width is the sum of per-letter widths, so kerning is ignored (the code comments call it "not precise").

5-state model (video/subtitle_clips_generator.py): line not narrated, then line narrating with word not narrated, word narrating, or word narrated, then line narrated.

Motion (animation/primitive_animation.py): only position, scale and opacity lambdas. Eased progress is clamped to [0,1], so overshoot has to be hand-built per primitive (pop_in_primitive.py, zoom_in_primitive.py, slide_in_primitive.py). There are 4 primitives and 9 presets. Triggers are in element_animator.py (narration-starts or narration-ends × word, line or segment, plus a tag_condition parsed from strings like "'a' and ('b' or 'c')" in tag/tag_condition.py). Missing: rotation, shake, blur, color or size tweens, and a moving highlight.

Emphasis (tag/tagger/semantic_tagger.py): regex over the whole-document text, wordlists (Unicode \w sanitizing, fine for Spanish), and AI rules through external_llm_tagger.py. The AI prompt asks for XML tags, and the response is discarded if the de-tagged text differs from the original. Any accent or punctuation change by the LLM therefore silently drops all AI tags.

Emoji:
- effect/text/emoji_in_segment_effect.py adds one emoji per segment as its own line above or below the segment. Rules: chance, max uses, no immediate repeat, max consecutive.
- The emoji comes from the pycaps.com API or OpenAI. emoji_in_segment_llm_getter.py makes 1 summary call plus 1 call per segment.
- effect/clip/animate_segment_emojis_effect.py swaps in animated Noto GIFs via AlphaVideoClip, downloaded at runtime with no checksum.
- emoji_in_word_effect.py appends a random emoji from a list after tagged runs. Its no-repeat option is dead code: last_used_emoji keeps a leading space, so the comparison never matches.

SFX: effect/sound/sound_effect.py plus builtin_sound.py (17 presets), with tag filter, offset and volume. 'custom' SFX from JSON crash the render (json_config_loader.py lines 124-133 pass what and when swapped, so _get_elements raises ValueError).

Typewriter (effect/clip/typewriting_effect.py): one bitmap per letter composited over time. Bug: it calls open_line(line, ElementState.WORD_BEING_NARRATED), so the line div gets the word-state class instead of `line-being-narrated`, and line-level CSS (e.g. retro-gaming's line background) differs between typewriter frames and full words.

Placement (layout/positions_calculator.py): x is always centered; y is top, center or bottom with an offset in [-1,1] (layout/definitions.py). Also max_width_ratio, min/max lines and word spacing. No face or safe-zone awareness.

Presets: 11 usable plus the empty `model` stub. hype (Komika font, yellow active word, zoom-in with overshoot, animated emoji), explosive (glow shadows, zoom plus slide, ding on AI 'highlighted' words), word-focus (orange box on the active word), neo-minimal (code-editor look, AI highlight), retro-gaming (typewriter), vibrant (pop-in, emoji). explosive and neo-minimal silently lose their emphasis without an API key.

Spanish: `--lang es` works. All LLM prompts are in English. The default whisper model is 'base'. External transcripts load via transcriber/transcript_loader.py (whisper_json / srt / vtt / pycaps_json). WhisperX word entries without start/end, common for numerals and symbols, are silently skipped (_parse_words_from_entries), so those words vanish from the captions unless you interpolate them first.
motion_graphics_detail: None. There are no kinetic-typography scenes, animated stats, lower thirds, icons, UI mockups or zoom punches on the underlying video. Nothing is LLM-authored as code (no Remotion, GSAP or HTML animation capture). CSS keyframes are frozen at screenshot time (playwright_screenshot_capturer.py, animations="disabled"), so writing CSS animations does not produce motion graphics. The only related assets are the SFX library (17 mp3 whooshes, hits and pops with tag and event triggers) and the animated Noto emoji overlays. Both are caption decorations, not B-roll. They could be donated to an MG layer, since the SFX triggers would suit MG entrances.
llm_integration_detail:
Internal LLM:
- ai/llm_provider.py defaults to Gpt().
- ai/gpt.py calls the OpenAI Responses API with gpt-4.1-mini using env PYCAPS_OPENAI_API_KEY; the openai package is not declared in any extra.
- If a pycaps API key is set (`pycaps config --set-api-key`, stored via ConfigService), AiTagger and EmojiInSegmentGetter prefer the proprietary service: api/api_sender.py POSTs {api_key, rendering_id, feature, payload with full transcript text} to http://pycaps.com/api/process. The endpoint answers 308 to HTTPS, so the key and transcript cross the first hop in cleartext.
- api_sender.py raises UnboundLocalError when the first attempt times out, because it logs response.status_code.

Injection: `LlmProvider.set(custom)` works from Python only, but the Llm ABC (ai/llm.py) declares `send_message(self, message, model)` while callers pass `prompt=` as a keyword (emoji_in_segment_llm_getter.py, utils/script_utils.py) or a single positional argument (external_llm_tagger.py). A subclass written to the ABC therefore raises TypeError. A Claude Code/Codex shim must copy Gpt's signature, `send_message(self, prompt, model=...)`.

There is no MCP, no skills, and no Claude Code or Codex wiring.

As a deterministic tool for a harness it is usable:
- CLI (cli/render_cli.py): `pycaps render --input --template|--config [--transcript whisperx.json --transcript-format] [--subtitle-data doc.json] [--style sel.prop=val] [--layout-align/--layout-align-offset] [--preview|--preview-time a,b] [--video-quality] [--lang/--whisper-model/--whisper-prompt]`, plus `pycaps preview-styles --template|--css`.
- Declarative JSON config (pipeline/json_schema.py, json_config_loader.py) that the brain can write.
- process_document saves `<output>.json` with every word's semantic_tags and structure_tags (pipeline/subtitle_data_service.py, common/models.py to_dict). With --subtitle-data, run() skips splitting, tagging and text effects but still runs clip effects (animated emoji), SFX and animators at render. The brain can therefore add 'highlighted' tags or insert emoji lines tagged `emoji-for-segment` directly in the JSON, with no API key.

Caveats:
- The CLI has no process-only or dry-run mode. The first pass to get the JSON is a full render, unless you use the Python API (prepare/transcribe/process_document).
- Later passes can be cheap: `--subtitle-data` plus `--preview-time a,b` renders just that window at low quality.
- `--preview` alone uses dummy text (PreviewTranscriber) and does not save JSON.
- Edited word text keeps its old line breaks and max_layout, because line splitting is skipped.
- `--style` crashes on values containing '.' (e.g. 1.5em), because `_parse_styles` splits on every '.'.

fit_rationale:
It is a poor base to fork for the whole editor: it covers only captions, and has no cutting, grade, stock B-roll or MG B-roll. Its render model (one source clip, captions composited on top, libx264 only, no alpha) would have to be rebuilt around a cut timeline. I lowered it from 3 to 2 because two of its supporting dimensions dropped: MG is 0 and render is 2.

As a donor or sidecar it is about 6/10. Because it burns captions onto any input video, the harness can run it last: cut, then grade, then B-roll/MG composite, then pycaps with a retimed transcript. The Claude Code/Codex brain writes the template JSON and edits tags and emoji in the subtitle JSON, so no OpenAI key is needed.

The CSS-per-word-state model with tags as classes, tag conditions, overshoot primitives, emoji pacing rules and SFX triggers are the right abstractions to borrow. To reach Captions.ai level you would need more motion primitives, real in-browser animation or frame-sequence capture, a gliding highlight, face- or safe-zone-aware placement, color tweens and alpha output. You would also need to fix the bugs listed here and strip the OpenAI and pycaps.com paths. Plan to own the fork.

Dependencies, verified via the GitHub API or pyproject:

Services: the optional pycaps.com API is a proprietary remote service with unknown terms.

Not present: Remotion (so no company-license threshold exposure), GSAP, and bundled ML weights (whisper weights download at runtime, MIT).

Caution: the pycaps README says the sibling tscaps is "engine MIT, app AGPL-3.0", and GitHub detects no license on tscaps. Copying tscaps app code would bring AGPL obligations.

summary:
VANTA is a marketing repo with one working Remotion demo. The README claims voice cloning, avatars, WhisperX captions, text-to-video, an editor, a timeline, 100+ transitions and motion graphics.

The only code that runs is one 15-second 1920x1080 self-promo (src/index.ts -> src/Root.tsx -> src/scenes/VantaShowcase.tsx). It is a logo reveal, a particle field, a clip-path word-wipe title, a hard-coded bar chart titled "integration readiness", a sine-wave "audio-reactive" waveform and feature cards.

I confirmed with grep that none of the 13 src/integrations/*.ts files is imported by any .tsx file. They are type shells with commented-out "how you would do it" code:
- animated-captions.ts: no AnimatedCaption component, even though its docstring shows one. getCaptionStyleCSS ignores the style. Its comment promises a binary search; the code is a linear scan.
- auto-captions.ts: POSTs to a hard-coded http://localhost:8000/transcribe. There is no WhisperX code.
- motion-graphics.ts: a linear lerp that ignores easing. lowerThird drops its text argument, and nothing renders to JSX.
- image-editor.ts: processImage returns width 0, height 0, size 0.
- vector-graphics.ts: booleanOperation returns its first input.
- transitions.ts: 3 GLSL snippets for 30 listed transition names. cube is truncated; pixelate and morph are near-complete gl-transitions ports. None is wired to anything.
- background-removal.ts: throws.
- ai-video, ai-avatar, voice-clone, ai-music: fetch() calls to servers the user must host.

There is no cutting, color grade, stock B-roll, LLM or agent integration, vertical format, or ingest of user footage.

On the user's question: if AutoBroll's captions fall short of Captions.ai, VANTA does not help. Its caption layer never renders a single frame. It has only type unions, 4 preset objects and one static CSS function (active word gold, scale 1.15, glow), which is below even a basic working gold-highlight caption. It has no per-word entrance animation, no emphasis detection, no emoji and no 9:16 safe-zone placement.

stack: A native macOS 15+ app for Apple Silicon only. Swift 6 with strict concurrency and SwiftUI, built with XcodeGen from project.yml. AVFoundation handles cutting and export, Vision does face detection, Core Image does the blur letterbox, and Core Animation burns in the hook overlay. WhisperKit large-v3 does transcription at segment level. In-process MLX LLMs: Gemma 4 12B (default) or Qwen 3.5 9B as the "Director", and Gemma 4 E4B for multimodal clip captioning. Upload-Post, a paid SaaS API, handles publishing and scheduling.

summary: Verified: this is a small, cleanly written native macOS app that turns a long 16:9 video into 3-6 shorts with social post copy. The flow: a sidecar .srt/.vtt or WhisperKit large-v3 transcript at segment level, then one in-process MLX LLM pass that returns a JSON list of 15-50 s clips (MomentFinderService). Each clip is cut as one continuous range (MediaExtractor.cutClip, passthrough export with a re-encode fallback). An optional 16:9 to 1080x1920 face-follow pan or blurred letterbox follows (VerticalReframer), then an optional static hook pill burned into the first 3 s (VideoOverlayRenderer), then publish or schedule through Upload-Post. On the user's question (AutoBroll has captions, just not Captions.ai-level ones), Shortcast cannot fill that gap. It never burns subtitles into the video. In this codebase "captions" means the TikTok/IG/YouTube post text and hashtags. The only on-video text is one fading hook pill, and the transcript carries no word timestamps. It also has no in-clip silence, filler or retake cutting, no color grade, no stock B-roll and no motion graphics. Its LLM is hard-wired to local MLX models. The original evaluation is accurate. My corrections are minor factual points plus one added red flag: a floating main-branch dependency with no lockfile.
captions_detail: Confirmed: no burned-in subtitles. Grepping the app for subtitle/karaoke/emoji/wordTimestamp finds only parseSubtitles (reading a sidecar .srt/.vtt as input) and 'dropSubtitle' (a UI label). The 'captions' are platform post copy. MomentFinderService.captioningPrompt asks for captions{tiktok,instagram,youtube}{hook,description,hashtags}. JSONVariantParser parses them. fit_rationale: A poor base for this goal, which confirms the original eval. Shortcast turns a long horizontal video into several shorts plus post copy. It does not polish an already vertical talking-head reel, and its reframe only runs on landscape clips. It covers none of the user's four needs: no in-clip silence, filler or retake cutting, no color grade, no burned-in captions of any kind (and only segment-level timestamps), and no stock or motion-graphics B-roll. Its LLM is hard-wired to in-process MLX models with no route for Claude Code or Codex. The stack is Swift/AVFoundation on macOS only, and the dependency graph floats on mlx-swift-lm main with no lockfile. Forking would mean keeping only the SwiftUI shell and rewriting everything that matters. It is useful only as a small donor of algorithms and prompts: the pan-path math, the moment-finder prompt with its JSON contract, the tolerant JSON salvage, the Whisper configuration lessons for Spanish, and the Upload-Post client.

red_flags: 'Captions' in this repo means social post text and hashtags. The app burns no subtitles into the video, so it offers nothing on the premium-captions gap.
No in-clip cutting (silence, filler, retakes). Each clip is one continuous range, and passthrough cuts snap to keyframes.
Segment-level transcription only (no word timestamps requested).
LLM is hard-wired to in-process MLX models (Gemma 4 12B, Qwen 3.5 9B, Gemma 4 E4B). No path for Claude Code, Codex, MCP or tool calling.
macOS 15+ and Apple Silicon only. The Swift/AVFoundation stack does not match an FFmpeg or Remotion/HTML harness.
New: project.yml tracks mlx-swift-lm at 'branch: main' and .gitignore excludes Package.resolved, so builds are not reproducible and may already break against current upstream.
Open model-load failures with no maintainer response: #6 (E4B fails to load) and #7 (weight shape mismatch). Also #4 'Too slow and not working', #3 'DMG damaged', #2 'Language defaults to Dutch'.
Single author, commits in a roughly 12-day window, no pushes since 2026-06-04.
No app tests. Releases are unsigned and un-notarized with hardened runtime off, and the README tells users to run xattr to strip quarantine.
Render path hard-codes 30 fps, and the blur plus hook path re-encodes twice.
Heavy runtime: a Director of about 7 GB (Gemma 12B) or 5 GB (Qwen) plus WhisperKit large-v3, downloaded at first use. The README says a 2-minute video takes minutes on an M1 Pro.
Gemma weights fall under Google's Gemma Terms of Use. Publishing depends on the paid Upload-Post SaaS.
Prompts are hard-coded in Spanish inside Swift string literals.
license_risks: Low for code reuse. The app code is Apache-2.0 (keep the NOTICE attribution if you copy it), and the vendored Gemma runtime and Gemma4Engine.swift are MIT. The SwiftPM deps are MIT or Apache-2.0. No Remotion, so no company-license threshold exposure. No GSAP. No proprietary binaries: model weights download at runtime from Hugging Face mlx-community. Model terms matter only if you reuse the model choices. Gemma 4 (12B, E4B) is under Google's Gemma Terms of Use and Prohibited Use Policy, which must pass through to downstream users. Qwen 3.5 9B is under its own open-weights license (check the HF card). Whisper weights are MIT. Upload-Post is a closed commercial API. The parts worth taking are small algorithms and prompts, so licensing is effectively a non-issue.
